newsitem.title: USA: Superhuman effort required to beat chess supercomputer.
newsitem.headline: Superhuman effort required to beat chess supercomputer.

text.p: Mentally and physically tired, world chess champion Garry Kasparov needs to make a superhuman effort this weekend if he is to defeat the machine Deep Blue in the closing games of their absorbing re-match.

The contest is tied after four games, just as it was in their 1996 clash in Philadelphia, but the momentum is with the improved and modified IBM supercomputer following many exhausting hours at the board and an uncharacteristic passivity from the Russian grandmaster.

"I think he is too concerned about who he is playing than with the games and he is not able to show his best because of that," said women's world champion Susan Polgar, one of three Hungarian sisters who play at grandmaster level.

The turning point for Kasparov came the day after Sunday's second encounter when analysis revealed that he had resigned in a drawn position, a remarkable miscalculation that had never happened before to the man respected as the best player in the history of the ancient game.

Instead of maintaining the lead in the match, it was tied at one win each. Two draws followed on Tuesday and Wednesday in which the system proved to be Kasparov's equal in almost every aspect of the game.

"I wasn't in a very good mood before the game because of obvious reasons," Kasparov said after the drawn fourth game. His psychological condition and his fading energy probably cost him a win and he had to agree to a draw Wednesday, according to expert observers.

Many grandmasters and hundreds of chess fans want to see the creative, swashbuckling Kasparov style return to the board for Saturday's fifth game, when he will play with the white pieces and the advantage of the first move for the last time in the $1.1 million contest. The sixth and final game is on Sunday when Deep Blue will play with white.

In the 12 years since becoming the youngest world champion in history at the age of 22, Kasparov has successfully defended world championship titles four times and out-thought, out-psyched and outplayed most of his opponents.

Kasparov's strongest motivation is his almost legendary desire to win and to survive whatever the challenge. He hates losing and it showed again in this match when he insinuated a slight of hand by the Deep Blue team in game two.

"It reminds me of the famous goal that Maradona scored against England in 86. He said it was 'the hand of God'," stated Kasparov, referring to a goal by one of the world's greatest soccer players, Diego Maradona of Argentina, in the 1986 World Cup in Mexico.
Maradona illegally fisted the ball into the net but the referee did not see the infraction and the goal counted.

"Suddenly you know it played like a God for one particular moment," said Kasparov, who will collect $700,000 if he wins the six-game match. The loser's prize is $400,000 and the total prize money will be shared in the event of a tie.

"You know Garry hates to lose and when he plays he's always playing to win and also he feels he is responsible for all other humans," said Ukrainian-born Anjelina Belakovskaia, the current United States women's chess champion.

The match, which is being held in a Manhattan skyscraper office complex, is part chess contest and part research project to help develop computers that can make complex, simultaneous calculations for applications such as weather forecasting, air traffic control and molecular dynamics.

Kasparov has opined that he is seeing "signs of intelligence" in Deep Blue and the computer's human-like style in the game that it won was regarded as the best-ever performance by a computer. But the project has nothing to do with artificial intelligence, according to IBM scientists.

Deep Blue is an IBM RS/6000 SP parallel processor with specialised microchips for chess. It can examine hundreds of millions of chess positions per second or 50 billion possibilities in three minutes, the average time it takes for a human to make a move in classical chess formats in which the game can last several hours.

More significant than its massive calculating powers has been the addition to the programme of more chess knowledge with the help of full-time grandmaster consultant Joel Benjamin, a former United States champion. And it also has no fear or other emotions that are important at all levels of competitive chess.

"After losing the first game, his opponent should have been exhausted the next day after not getting much sleep and demoralised by the defeat, but Deep Blue wasn't, it's a machine and that's the advantage it has," said chess computer researcher Frederic Friedel, one of Kasparov's closest advisors.
